name: Galileo astronomical telescopes
summary: Galileo built a series of increasingly powerful telescopes, grinding or choosing his own lenses, good enough to study the Moon and later the planets.
description: Galileo's progressively improved convex-objective/concave-eyepiece telescopes, with selected or manufactured lenses adequate for his lunar and later planetary observations.
tier_reason: The scoped record is a particular configuration, local witness, trial or material application. Dependence across fields or generations on THIS referent is not established; do not inherit the importance of its broader missing family.
why: News of the Dutch spyglass reached Venice in 1609, and Galileo, already an instrument maker, set out to build a better one.

date.label: November–December 1609
date.basis: Museum dates the lunar watercolours to November–December 1609.

events.statement: Galileo used an improved telescope in a sustained program of observations and lunar drawings.
events.scope: Galileo’s telescope configuration used for the lunar observing series, with later iterations not treated as the same individual instrument.
events.caveats: The exact telescope used for every lunar drawing is not separately identified; later Jupiter instruments need not be identical.

evidence.locator: Object title and description, Ms. Gal. 48 f. 28r
evidence.supports: Dates the drawings to November–December and says they were made from telescopic observation.

evidence.locator: Van Helden, printed pp. 188–189 / PDF pp. 194–195
evidence.supports: Discusses Galileo’s progressively improved telescope configurations.

date.basis: Construction and improvement ran from 1609 into early 1610; lunar and planetary observing configurations were attained at different points.

events.statement: Galileo's progressively improved convex-objective/concave-eyepiece telescopes, with selected or manufactured lenses adequate for his lunar and later planetary observations.
events.caveats: A sequence of instruments, not one unchanged telescope. Claimed thirty-power performance is not adopted as a measured specification of the discovery instrument.

evidence.locator: Albert Van Helden, Galileo and the telescope, printed pp. 183, 188–189 (PDF pp. 189, 194–195)
evidence.supports: Distinguishes late-1609 lunar work from early-1610 planetary capability and documents lens-making effort.

evidence.locator: Original fols.6r–6v; translation printed pp. 10–11 (PDF pp. 11–12)
evidence.supports: Describes lens arrangement and progressive instrument improvement.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest defensible dated record of this scoped referent in the retained evidence; later community entry is recorded separately. community_entry.community: Galileo’s astronomical observing practice in Padua
community_entry.rationale: Astronomical data gathering is actual specialist use even though Galileo helped make the instrument.
community_entry.caveats: The exact telescope used for every lunar drawing is not separately identified; later Jupiter instruments need not be identical.

caveats: A sequence of instruments, not one unchanged telescope. Claimed thirty-power performance is not adopted as a measured specification of the discovery instrument.

links.statement: News of a Dutch spyglass, confirmed from Paris, prompted Galileo to make and improve a similar instrument.
links.scope: Dutch Republic–Paris–Republic of Venice, 1608–1610; communication and adaptation rather than transfer of one identified specimen.
links.alternatives: Other makers and observers obtained or made spyglasses independently of Galileo.
links.caveats: The Dutchman is unnamed in Galileo's account; this is not a proven personal Lipperhey-to-Galileo contact or object chain.
links.timing: The public Dutch episode in 1608 precedes Galileo's 1609 construction; later improvements continue into 1610.

evidence.locator: Original fol.6r; translation printed p. 10 (PDF p. 11)
evidence.supports: Galileo identifies the Dutch report, Badovere's confirmation, and his subsequent construction.

evidence.locator: Albert Van Helden, Galileo and the telescope, printed pp. 183, 186–187 (PDF pp. 189, 192–193)
evidence.supports: Places the report in documented circulation and discusses uncertainty about what Galileo had seen.
